item.title: Polarization-dependent exchange effects in intrabeam scattering
item.description: arXiv:2610.24245v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The emittance growth due to intrabeam scattering (IBS) depends on the scattering cross section and is therefore affected by the exchange interaction of identical particles. However, as the IBS growth rates are typically dominated by small-angle scattering events and the exchange interaction only significantly alters the cross section at relatively large angles, the influence of the exchange interaction is usually small. In this paper, we calculate the small corrections to the growth rates resulting from the exchange interaction. We include the polarization dependence of the exchange term in the cross section, and so we also present the growth rates as a function of the beam polarization.
item.dc:creator: Joseph P. Devlin, Georg H. Hoffstaetter

item.title: Scaling laws for contamination traversal times during vacuum breaks in superconducting accelerators
item.description: arXiv:2610.24876v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A sudden loss of vacuum in a superconducting radio-frequency (SRF) accelerator drives warm gas into the evacuated beamline, where it propagates through interconnected SRF cavities cooled by liquid helium, causing surface contamination, intense heat deposition, and dangerous pressure buildup. Yet predicting how such a failure propagates through realistic multicell cavities has remained difficult because compressible gas dynamics, condensation and cryogenic heat transfer are strongly coupled. Here we develop and experimentally validate a multidimensional computational framework that resolves these processes, and apply it to a full-scale nine-cell SRF cavity. We find that the repeated cell geometry produces staircase-like gas-front propagation, as impingement, recirculation and localized cryopumping strongly retard the bulk flow within each cell. Across a broad range of breach sizes, the cavity traversal time follows a robust power-law scaling with leakage area, providing quantitative guidance for the response time of beamline isolation and protection systems. The simulations also reveal a geometry-confined Mach disk whose position and size track the advancing gas front, suggesting that its acoustic emission could potentially enable rapid, non-invasive detection and localization of vacuum failures. These findings pave the way for a new generation of predictive diagnostics and protection strategies to safeguard large-scale superconducting accelerators.
item.dc:creator: Yinghe Qi, Qutadah Rababah, Wei Guo

item.title: Construction of crystal-based light sources with LWFA electron beams
item.description: arXiv:2610.25336v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We discuss a possibility to construct a crystal-based light source (CLS) of gamma-rays using electron beams produce by Laser Wake Field Acceleration (LWFA). This state-of-the-art acceleration technique is capable of producing few-GeV, ultra-short (fs) electron beams. In the case studies presented, we demonstrate the feasibility of novel gamma-ray CLSs based on exposing single crystals to electron beams available at the ELI-ELBA. The results of rigorous numerical simulations are presented to characterise the radiation emitted emitted by 1 and 4 GeV electrons incident on a 200-micron-thick single silicon crystal along the (110) plane. The simulations were performed using the current divergence as well as a smaller value that is believed to be a realistic to achieve in the near future. We demonstrate that it is feasible to achieve a photon yield of $10^6-10^7$ photons/s in the photon energy range from 5 to 50 MeV. Looking further ahead, we also performed a similar analysis for a 4-GeV positron beam incident on much thicker targets, up to 2 mm oriented silicon crystal. In this case, the photon yield can be increased by an order of magnitude.

item.title: A General Treatment of Coupled Cavity Resonators
item.description: arXiv:2610.25648v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Consider several cavity resonators whose resonant frequencies and electromagnetic fields are known, and suppose that they are coupled through apertures. How can the resonant frequencies and resonant electromagnetic fields of the resulting coupled-cavity resonator be expressed in terms of the original resonant frequencies and electromagnetic fields? This is a problem frequently encountered in radio-frequency systems for accelerators. One example is a multicell cavity used in high-energy electron accelerators. In this note, the resonant frequencies and resonant electromagnetic fields of such coupled cavities are examined as generally as possible, based only on Maxwell's equations and boundary conditions. Specifically, the response function of a cavity as viewed from its coupling ports, namely, its admittance matrix, is derived, and a formulation is developed to express the coupled resonant electromagnetic fields using this matrix. The resulting formulation shows that the coupled resonant modes can be described in terms of overlap integrals between the resonant modes of the cavities and the waveguide modes at the coupling apertures. It also shows that the coupled resonant frequencies are given by the zeros of the determinant of a matrix constructed from the admittance matrices. The results thus obtained are applied to simple systems to confirm the validity of the formulation. Numerical calculations based on this formulation are also carried out for periodic systems in an attempt to derive dispersion relations.
item.dc:creator: Osamu Kamigaito

item.title: Modeling and control of traveling wave structures with arbitrary beam loading
item.description: arXiv:2610.26616v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traveling wave (TW) structures are widely used in linear or circular accelerators for beam acceleration. Unlike the standing wave cavities, the overall accelerating voltage cannot be measured by the probes installed in the TW structures. This creates difficulties measuring and regulating the accelerating voltage and phase felt by the beam when it passes through the structure. In this paper, a model of TW structures is developed, allowing us to estimate the accelerating voltage and phase from the measurement of the RF drive power input to the TW structure. The beam loading effects, i.e., the beam-induced accelerating voltage and phase in the TW structure, are also included in the model. With the TW structure model, control methods are proposed to stabilize the accelerating voltage and phase felt by the beam based on feedback, feedforward, and optimization. The validity of the TW structure model is confirmed with the test results at the SwissFEL with improved beam stability under the same RF feedback controller. This work provides a firm basis for developing the multiple-bunch operation strategy for SwissFEL required by the future upgrade with more beamlines.
item.dc:creator: Zheqiao Geng, Riccardo Zennaro, Alessandro Citterio

item.title: SynradG4: A Geant4-Based Extension for Synchrotron Radiation Background Studies in the ePIC Detector at the Electron-Ion Collider
item.description: arXiv:2408.11709v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) will operate at high luminosity with multi-GeV, high-current electron beams, resulting in substantial synchrotron radiation (SR) emission in the electron storage ring (ESR). A detailed understanding of SR photon transport in the complex three-dimensional interaction region (IR) geometry is critical for estimating backgrounds in the ePIC detector and for developing effective shielding and masking strategies. This paper presents SynradG4, an EIC-specific extension of Geant4 for fast photon tracking in vacuum based on established models of SR reflection and rough-surface scattering. SynradG4 integrates the specular and diffuse photon reflection models of Synrad+ into the Geant4 geometry and field framework, while disabling all bulk matter interactions to achieve high-statistics transport through the 50-m-long IR vacuum system. The absorbed photons are then passed to a second-stage DD4hep simulation, in which electromagnetic processes such as photoabsorption, Compton scattering, Rayleigh scattering, and fluorescence are enabled for their propagation through the beam pipe and detector materials. SynradG4 is not intended to replace general SR simulation codes; rather, it complements them by providing the workflow and geometry integration capabilities needed for EIC-specific background studies. Benchmark tests show that SynradG4 reproduces Synrad+ to within about 1% for both specular and diffuse reflection, and that it agrees well with Synrad3D and with the native Geant4 X-ray reflection model for smooth surfaces. Using the full IR geometry and machine lattice, we present the first SR background estimates for the ePIC detector and evaluate the impact of potential SR masks.
item.dc:creator: Andrii Natochii

item.title: Thermal Decoherence and Population Transfer of MeV Channeling Electrons in Diamond
item.description: arXiv:2602.16529v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Channeling radiation from MeV-regime electrons is governed by transitions between quantized transverse bound states, but experimental spectra are strongly modified by thermal diffuse scattering. To capture these open-system dynamics, a frozen-phonon multislice framework is combined with bound-state projection analysis to construct depth-dependent reduced density matrices in selected transverse manifolds. Beyond reproducing experimental channeling-radiation transition energies, this approach separates thermal population transfer, intra-manifold decoherence, and cross-manifold coherence loss. Applied to 16.9 MeV axial electron channeling in $\langle100\rangle$ diamond, the results show approximately exponential population decay from the initially occupied states, accompanied by strongly channel-dependent feeding among low-lying manifolds. Starting from a coherent superposition within the degenerate 2p manifold, stochastic symmetry breaking by thermal displacements drives the intra-manifold purity toward the maximally mixed limit, indicating rapid phase scrambling. Under 1s initialization, population transferred into the 2p and 3d manifolds remains internally close to maximally mixed, yet a weak residual 2p-3d cross-manifold coherence persists. This framework goes beyond static mean-field thermal broadening and provides a microscopic basis for evaluating population dynamics and coherence lifetimes in strongly quantized channeling-radiation systems.
